newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Fuel costs could rattle BA result.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Fuel costs could rattle BA result.

text.p: British Airways Plc is expected to follow up last year's record profits with a further rise for the half-year headline result when it reports next Tuesday.
But analysts say underlying operating profits are likely to be hit by the hike in fuel prices and there are fears that the profits machine is starting to rattle after a five-year climb.

Market forecasts are for pretax profits for the six months to September 30 of around 460 million stg, up from 430 million stg last time, accompanied by an increase in the dividend to 4.25 from 3.85 on earnings up six percent at around 35.8p.

Traffic was up 4.6 percent in the half year and, while a 6.8 percent increase in capacity pushed average loadings down 1.7 points to 75.2 percent of capacity, BA says lucrative business and first class seats have been filling at a faster rate than those at the cheaper end of the aircraft.

Current market forecasts predict pretax profits for the full year to end-March 1997 to jump to between 620 and 705 million stg, up from 585 million stg for last year, and for the dividend to increase 9.8 percent to 15p on earnings of around 48 pence.
Analysts say generally BA's prospects remain bright as world demand for air travel continues to rise each year.
"Capacity should remain tight and the upward march on (average fare) yields should continue," said Mike Powell of NatWest Markets.

BA is pressing ahead with its strategy of developing a global "hub and spoke" network, traffic continues to grow and chief executive Robert Ayling has vowed to make radical cuts in overheads with his "Step Change" plan.

He threatens to hive off ancillary operations to outside contractors and to keep staff numbers down by paying off 5,000 people, or nearly 10 percent of the workforce, to make way for a similar number of new recruits with different skills.
"We have got a long term positive view on the share," said Mike Stoddart of brokers Charterhouse-Tilney.
"They are going to grow the operation with flat staff numbers so that should boost the productivity hugely," he said.
"There are always short term doubts on something like this but whatever the figures are next week we think that there is still good growth to come."

But the short term outlook has been clouded by several factors. Fuel costs have shot up, sterling's strength could hit the value of sales overseas, and BA has the added costs this year of creating a second London hub at Gatwick, analysts said.
"All airline stocks are overshadowed at the moment by what has happened to the oil price," said Powell. "It's a very hefty increase which comes straight off the margin."

Airlines say jet fuel prices have jumped by as much as 40 percent from a year ago and earlier this week The International Air Transport Association (IATA) called for an meeting of the world's airlines on November 13 to discuss the 10 percent overall rise in fuel prices so far this year.
BA's fuel and oil bill last year amounted to 655 million stg, accounting for 9.3 percent of all costs.

Meanwhile, controversy rages on over BA's proposed alliance with American Airlines, which has also alienated BA's existing transAtlantic partner USAir, and there are also concerns about BA's bid for ailing French carrier Air Liberte.

The half-year result will also suffer from disruption to services caused by a UK pilots' pay dispute in July but will be helped by lower borrowing costs and backpayment of preference dividends due on its investment in USAir.
Guy Kekwick of Lehman Brothers says he expects BA to book in an exceptional $35 million in backpayments from USAir in the second quarter.
However, a likely drop in first-half operating profits to 493 million stg from 523 million stg a year ago makes him cautious for the future.
"This is the first time we have seen operating profits at BA down quarter on quarter for over three years," Kekwick said in a recent research note.
-- Greg Mahlich, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
